LIABILITY OF A PURPORTED PARTNER — WHEN SOMEONE WHO IS NOT A PARTNER IS HELD LIABLE AS ONE (CORP. CODE §§ 16306(A), 16307(C)–(E), 16308; ARMATO V. BADEN; J. C. WATTENBARGER & SONS V. SANDERS; MOEN V. ART’S CAFE; INGLEWOOD TEACHERS ASSN. V. PERB) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Dana Ruiz · Harbor Lane Builders

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet concerns Dana Ruiz, who is described as having been associated in some way with Harbor Lane Builders without being an actual partner in it, and the representation at issue, described as: name listed on the shop door and on invoices. The person said to have dealt with the business in reliance on that representation is identified here as Coastal Supply Co. Prepared January 5, 2027.

The subject is Cal. Corp. Code § 16308, the purported-partner section of the California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, together with the two neighbouring sections in the same article that set the baseline it departs from (§ 16306, the liability of actual partners) and the enforcement rules that expressly reach it (§ 16307). Section 16308 does not ask whether a partnership exists. It states when a person who is not a partner at all can be held liable as though he or she were one, because of a representation made or consented to and relied upon by someone who then dealt with the actual or purported firm.

This project's existing Business Formation documents approach partnership from the other direction. The General Partnership Agreement and Joint Ventures sheets describe when the conduct of actual co-owners forms a partnership by operation of law under § 16202; the Statement of Partnership Authority sheet describes the filing; the Piercing the Corporate Veil sheet describes reaching an owner behind an entity. None of them addresses liability imposed on a non-partner by § 16308. This sheet states what the section says and what the California decisions that discuss the doctrine have held. It does not evaluate whether Dana Ruiz is liable to Coastal Supply Co., and it is not legal advice.

THE CORE RULE OF CORPORATIONS CODE SECTION 16308
Cal. Corp. Code § 16308 opens with a carve-out and then states the rule. The carve-out is in the section's first line: the section applies “Except with respect to registered limited liability partnerships and foreign limited liability partnerships.” Subdivision (a) then states the operative rule. Two things trigger it — a person who “by words or conduct, purports to be a partner,” or a person who “consents to being represented by another as a partner.” The representation may be of partnership “in a partnership” that actually exists, or “with one or more persons not partners,” that is, in a firm that does not exist at all. The consequence runs to “a person to whom the representation is made,” and only if that person, “relying on the representation, enters into a transaction with the actual or purported partnership.” The statute thus states three elements on its face: a representation of partnership by or with the consent of the person sought to be charged, reliance by the claimant, and a transaction entered into with the actual or purported partnership.

REPRESENTATIONS MADE “IN A PUBLIC MANNER” AND THE UNAWARE PURPORTED PARTNER
The second sentence of Cal. Corp. Code § 16308(a) states a separate and broader rule for representations made publicly. Where the representation — made “either by the purported partner or by a person with the purported partner’s consent” — “is made in a public manner,” the statute extends liability to “a person who relies upon the purported partnership even if the purported partner is not aware of being held out as a partner to the claimant.” The distinction the sentence draws is about who the claimant is, not about what was said: under the first sentence the claimant must be a person “to whom the representation is made,” while under the public-manner sentence the claimant need only be a person who relied, and the purported partner's unawareness of that particular claimant does not defeat the claim. The purported partner's consent to the representation is still part of the sentence's own terms where another person made it.

HOW MUCH THE PURPORTED PARTNER OWES: TWO DIFFERENT MEASURES
The last two sentences of Cal. Corp. Code § 16308(a) set the measure of the purported partner's liability, and they differ according to whether a partnership liability arose at all. Where “partnership liability results,” the statute makes the purported partner “liable with respect to that liability as if the purported partner were a partner” — the measure is borrowed from the liability of a real partner. Where “no partnership liability results,” the statute instead makes the purported partner “liable with respect to that liability jointly and severally with any other person consenting to the representation.” In the second case the co-obligors are not partners either: they are the other persons who consented to the same representation.

SUBDIVISION (B): THE PURPORTED PARTNER AS AGENT OF THOSE WHO CONSENTED
Cal. Corp. Code § 16308(b) addresses the liability of the people on the other side of the representation — those who consented to a non-partner being held out as a partner. Where a person “is thus represented to be a partner in an existing partnership, or with one or more persons not partners,” the statute makes that purported partner “an agent of persons consenting to the representation to bind them to the same extent and in the same manner as if the purported partner were a partner, with respect to persons who enter into transactions in reliance upon the representation.” The subdivision then splits according to how many of an existing firm's partners consented. If “all of the partners of the existing partnership consent to the representation, a partnership act or obligation results” — the obligation is the firm's. If “fewer than all” consented, “the person acting and the partners consenting to the representation are jointly and severally liable,” and the statute does not make it a partnership obligation.

TWO THINGS THAT DO NOT MAKE A PERSON A PURPORTED PARTNER: BEING NAMED IN A FILING, AND NOT FILING
Cal. Corp. Code § 16308(c) and (d) each remove a filing-based route to purported-partner liability. Subdivision (c) states that “A person is not liable as a partner merely because the person is named by another in a statement of partnership authority” — the public Secretary of State filing that this project's Statement of Partnership Authority information sheet describes. Subdivision (d) addresses the opposite situation, a person who has left: “A person does not continue to be liable as a partner merely because of a failure to file a statement of dissociation or to amend a statement of partnership authority to indicate the partner’s dissociation from the partnership.” Both subdivisions use the word “merely,” so each removes the filing as a sufficient basis standing alone rather than as a fact a court may consider.

A comparable result was reached under predecessor law on a different filing. In Armato v. Baden the Court of Appeal described the earlier holding of J. C. Wattenbarger & Sons v. Sanders as being “that a limited partner defendant was not an ostensible general partner merely because the fictitious partnership certificate listed his name without a designation that he was a limited partner.”

SUBDIVISION (E): THE CLOSING NEGATIVE RULE, AND THE SECTION'S ENACTMENT HISTORY
Cal. Corp. Code § 16308 closes by confining itself. Subdivision (e) states: “Except as otherwise provided in subdivisions (a) and (b), persons who are not partners as to each other are not liable as partners to other persons.” The general rule of California partnership law is therefore that non-partners are not liable as partners, and subdivisions (a) and (b) are the stated exceptions to it.

Both publishers print the same enactment line at the end of the section: “(Added by Stats. 1996, Ch. 1003, Sec. 2. Effective January 1, 1997.)” Neither publisher shows any later amendment. The Legislative Counsel's display places the section in Article 3 (“Relations of Partners to Persons Dealing with Partnership”) of Chapter 5, the Uniform Partnership Act of 1994.

THE TWO NEIGHBOURING SECTIONS: ACTUAL-PARTNER LIABILITY, AND COLLECTING A JUDGMENT
Section 16308 borrows its measure of liability from the rule that governs real partners, which is set out two sections earlier. Cal. Corp. Code § 16306(a) provides: “Except as otherwise provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), all partners are liable jointly and severally for all obligations of the partnership unless otherwise agreed by the claimant or provided by law.” Reading the two sections together, § 16308(a)'s phrase “as if the purported partner were a partner” points at the joint and several liability § 16306(a) imposes. The difference between them is what must be proved: § 16306(a) applies to persons who are partners and requires no proof of any representation or of reliance, while § 16308 applies to persons who are not partners and requires both.

The section in between governs suits and judgments, and it states in terms that it reaches purported-partner obligations. Cal. Corp. Code § 16307(e) provides: “This section applies to any partnership liability or obligation resulting from a representation by a partner or purported partner under Section 16308.” What that draws in includes § 16307(c): “A judgment against a partnership is not by itself a judgment against a partner. A judgment against a partnership may not be satisfied from a partner’s assets unless there is also a judgment against the partner.” The same section's subdivision (d) lists the five circumstances in which a judgment creditor of a partner may levy on that partner's own assets for a partnership claim, beginning with a returned-unsatisfied writ of execution against the partnership.

THE ONE PUBLISHED CALIFORNIA APPELLATE DECISION THAT CITES SECTION 16308
Armato v. Baden (1999) 71 Cal.App.4th 885 is, on the searching done for this sheet, the only published decision of the California Supreme Court or Court of Appeal that cites Corporations Code § 16308. The plaintiff had been treated at a medical group by a physician assistant and sued four doctors who worked there as independent contractors but who had never treated her. The court framed the issue as “apparently one of first impression in California, whether an independent contractor of a professional service corporation which permits his name and status to be associated with the corporation creates an ‘ostensible partnership’ so as to make him liable for the torts of the corporation’s employee.”

The opinion's citation of § 16308 is a mapping of old law to new. Addressing the predecessor statute, the court wrote that “Respondents point out that Corporations Code former section 15016, pertaining to partners by estoppel (see now Corp. Code, § 16308, using the term ‘purported partner’), deals with the issue of partners by estoppel; however, the statutory requirements therein are not met in this case.” The case arose from 1994–95 events and was therefore decided under former § 15016, not under § 16308.

Code § 16308, the purported-partner section of the California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, together with the two neighbouring sections in the same article that set the baseline it departs from (§ 16306, the liability of actual partners) and the enforcement rules that expressly reach it (§ 16307). Section 16308 does not ask whether a partnership exists. It states when a person who is not a partner at all can be held liable as though he or she were one, because of a representation made or consented to and relied upon by someone who then dealt with the actual or purported firm.

This project's existing Business Formation documents approach partnership from the other direction. The General Partnership Agreement and Joint Ventures sheets describe when the conduct of actual co-owners forms a partnership by operation of law under § 16202; the Statement of Partnership Authority sheet describes the filing; the Piercing the Corporate Veil sheet describes reaching an owner behind an entity. Cal. Corp. Code § 16308 opens with a carve-out and then states the rule. The carve-out is in the section's first line: the section applies “Except with respect to registered limited liability partnerships and foreign limited liability partnerships.” Subdivision (a) then states the operative rule. Two things trigger it — a person who “by words or conduct, purports to be a partner,” or a person who “consents to being represented by another as a partner.” The representation may be of partnership “in a partnership” that actually exists, or “with one or more persons not partners,” that is, in a firm that does not exist at all. The consequence runs to “a person to whom the representation is made,” and only if that person, “relying on the representation, enters into a transaction with the actual or purported partnership.” The statute thus states three elements on its face: a representation of partnership by or with the consent of the person sought to be charged, reliance by the claimant, and a transaction entered into with the actual or purported partnership.

If “all of the partners of the existing partnership consent to the representation, a partnership act or obligation results” — the obligation is the firm's. If “fewer than all” consented, “the person acting and the partners consenting to the representation are jointly and severally liable,” and the statute does not make it a partnership obligation.

Section 16308 borrows its measure of liability from the rule that governs real partners, which is set out two sections earlier. Cal. Corp. Code § 16306(a) provides: “Except as otherwise provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), all partners are liable jointly and severally for all obligations of the partnership unless otherwise agreed by the claimant or provided by law.” Reading the two sections together, § 16308(a)'s phrase “as if the purported partner were a partner” points at the joint and several liability § 16306(a) imposes. The difference between them is what must be proved: § 16306(a) applies to persons who are partners and requires no proof of any representation or of reliance, while § 16308 applies to persons who are not partners and requires both.

The section in between governs suits and judgments, and it states in terms that it reaches purported-partner obligations. Cal. Corp. Code § 16307(e) provides: “This section applies to any partnership liability or obligation resulting from a representation by a partner or purported partner under Section 16308.” What that draws in includes § 16307(c): “A judgment against a partnership is not by itself a judgment against a partner. A judgment against a partnership may not be satisfied from a partner’s assets unless there is also a judgment against the partner.” The same section's subdivision (d) lists the five circumstances in which a judgment creditor of a partner may levy on that partner's own assets for a partnership claim, beginning with a returned-unsatisfied writ of execution against the partnership.

Art’s Cafe (1950) 95 Cal.App.2d 577 — decided under former Civil Code § 2410, which the opinion notes was “now incorporated in Corp. Baden quoted the first of these sentences in 1999.

The California materials use several labels for the doctrine interchangeably. The statute calls the person a “purported partner”; the older decisions say “ostensible partner,” “ostensible partnership” or “partner by estoppel.” Armato addressed the point in a footnote: “On this appeal, we also deem to be essentially interchangeable the terms ostensible partnership, apparent partnership, purported partnership, and partnership by estoppel.” A reader searching for California authority will find it under all four names, and under the former statutory sections (Civil Code § 2410, then Corporations Code § 15016) as well as under § 16308.
